task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: How do earthquake early warning systems work, and what can and can't they do? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of September 10, 2024. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Earthquake early warning systems detect the first seismic waves from a fault rupture and calculate predicted shaking intensity at distant locations before destructive shaking arrives.
Earthquakes produce two types of seismic waves: P-waves, which travel faster but cause less damage, and S-waves, which travel slower but carry most of the destructive shaking energy.
Early warning systems detect P-waves and use them to estimate the earthquake's magnitude and location; the warning is then transmitted electrically, which travels faster than the slower S-waves.
The time between a warning and the arrival of damaging shaking can range from a few seconds in nearby areas to more than a minute for locations far from the epicenter.
Areas near the epicenter receive no warning because S-waves arrive before the system can process the P-wave data and transmit an alert — a limitation called the 'blind zone.'
Warning times of even five to ten seconds allow automated systems to slow trains, open fire station doors, stop industrial equipment, and alert surgeons to pause procedures.
The ShakeAlert system, operated by the United States Geological Survey, covers California, Oregon, and Washington state using about 1,500 seismic sensors.

Japan's early warning system, which dates to the early 2000s, has the most extensive operational experience; it sent an alert approximately 90 seconds before strong shaking reached a major population center during a catastrophic magnitude 9.0 subduction earthquake, giving residents and transit operators time to take protective action.

Seismologist Dr. Kwame Osei of Pacific Basin University said: "The goal is not to prevent an earthquake. It is to give automated systems and prepared individuals a window to take a protective action."
False alerts — warnings sent for events that do not produce damaging shaking — erode public trust over time; systems are designed to minimize false alarms, but there is a tradeoff with sensitivity.
Cell phone emergency alert systems can deliver warnings to millions of people simultaneously without requiring a separate app; the alert sounds regardless of whether the phone is silenced.
Sensor density is critical: more sensors reduce the blind zone and improve magnitude estimation accuracy; adding sensors also increases maintenance cost.
Early warning cannot predict an earthquake before it starts; the warning is issued only after rupture has begun.
The most effective individual response upon receiving an alert is drop, cover, and hold on under a sturdy surface — the window may be too short for evacuation.
Dr. Osei said research is ongoing to use new machine-learning methods to estimate final magnitude from the first half-second of P-wave data, which would extend warning times.

High-rise buildings with longer natural sway periods experience different shaking dynamics than low buildings; early warning systems can in principle trigger building-specific responses if the structure is instrumented.
Magnitude estimates improve as the rupture progresses and more sensors report data; an initial alert may be updated within seconds.
Countries without dense sensor networks — much of Latin America, Africa, and Southeast Asia — lack functional early warning coverage despite high seismic risk.
The cost of the ShakeAlert network, including sensors, software, and integration with emergency alert systems, was approximately $460 million as of 2023.

Dr. Osei said the practical limit on warning time is physics, not technology: in a megathrust earthquake directly beneath a city, even perfect detection would provide no warning to residents above the fault.

a warning time stated as guaranteed for any location
a Japan-specific alert time different from 90 seconds
